item.title: Lecture: The Placebo Puzzle
item.summary: A lecture on the placebo effect: what expectation can and cannot change, why drug trials need a placebo group, and the ethics of prescribing one.
item.transcript_text: Let me begin with a puzzle that has troubled medicine for a very long time. Give a patient a pill that contains nothing active, a sugar pill, tell them it will ease their pain, and a surprising proportion will report that it does. This is the placebo effect, and it's tempting to dismiss it as people simply imagining things. I'd caution against that. Pain, nausea and fatigue are, to a considerable degree, experiences shaped by the brain, and expectation appears to be one of the things that shapes them. When we expect relief, the brain may well respond in ways that genuinely change what we feel. Note, though, what the placebo effect doesn't do, at least as far as the current evidence suggests. It doesn't shrink a tumour or mend a broken bone. Its influence seems to be largely on symptoms, on how we experience an illness, rather than on the illness itself. Now, this creates a genuine methodological problem. If almost any treatment can produce some improvement purely through expectation, how do we know whether a new drug actually works? Hence the controlled trial, in which one group receives the drug and another receives a placebo, ideally with neither the patients nor the doctors knowing who got which. Only if the drug outperforms the placebo do we credit it with an effect of its own. And then there's the ethical puzzle, which I personally find the most interesting part. If expectation helps, should a doctor ever prescribe a placebo knowingly? Deceiving patients, even kindly, undermines the trust that medicine depends on. Intriguingly, some researchers have explored so-called open-label placebos, where patients are told quite plainly that the pill is inactive. Whether that works reliably remains, I'd stress, an open question.

It is too simple an explanation.
It explains why placebos cure illness.
